title: Multi-tenant Noise Injection Benchmark Protocol
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary

This document defines the Multi-tenant Noise Injection Benchmark Protocol (MNIBP) used by the runtime team to quantify how different types of noisy neighbor behavior and kernel-level jitter affect per-tenant SLOs, cost-per-token, and model fidelity. The goal is to produce reproducible, comparable results across GPU types and scheduler configurations so we can: 1) validate scheduler hardening and isolation features, 2) estimate degradation risk for customer SLAs, and 3) generate test vectors for release gates.

Scope

- Applies to runtime clusters supporting multi-tenant inference (hosted + Dedicated pools).
- Tests cover kernel scheduling policies, preemption waveforms, KV-cache eviction, and bursty tenant load shapes.
- Not intended for hardware failure injection (use the Hardware Fault Simulation Playbook).

Owners and Contacts

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime / Performance & Benchmarking subteam
- Document steward: Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood.example.com)
- Escalation: Marcus Chen (runtime SRE) for test infra; Lena Rodredguez for kernel scheduler changes

High-level test objectives

1) Isolation fidelity: measure how a noisy tenant increases P95 and P99 latencies for co-located tenants.
2) Degradation envelope: map resource contention -> fidelity drop (e.g., top-k token divergence, hallucination rate on eval prompts).
3) Recovery behavior: validate bounded-degradation and automatic fallback thresholds restore SLOs within configured time windows.

Test matrix and scenarios

We run the following scenario classes across GPU families (A100/80GB, H100, and third-party accelerators where supported):

- BurstStorm: a synthetic tenant emits microbursts (100 requests in 500ms) at high concurrency to exercise preemption and batch-slicing.
- KVWarmThump: repeated short sessions that thrash KV cache by swapping hot prefixes across many tenants.
- KernelNoisemaker: run a co-located micro-benchmark designed to introduce variable kernel latency (sleeps, heavy scatter-gather kernels) to emulate driver or kernel jitter.
- MemoryShrinker: allocate transient large-memory allocations to force cross-tenant eviction and compaction events.
- IOBackpressure: saturate network/GPU DMA channels to measure pipeline head-of-line effects.

Each scenario is parameterized. Example parameters (expandable):

- duration: 180s | 600s | 3600s
- noisy_tenant_load: 0.25 | 0.5 | 1.0 normalized to baseline throughput
- concurrency_profiles: [{short: 1-4}, {medium: 8-32}, {long-tail: 64-256}]
- model_shapes: text-gen (2k context), chat (multi-turn), embeddings (batch 64)

Test environment configuration table

| key | recommended value | notes |
|-----|-------------------|-------|
| cluster_tag | perf-mnibp-<gpu>-v1 | Isolated cluster snapshot used for the run |
| scheduler_profile | slo-aware-priority-v2 | Includes preemption hysteresis and kernel-credit caps |
| kvcache_policy | lru-ttl-120s | TTL tuned to workload; change only for KVWarmThump runs |
| quota_isolation | tenant-cpu:1 vgpu:0.5 | Baseline resource caps for noisy tenants |
| telemetry_level | verbose-trace | Required for attribution (kernel + request trace) |

Pre-test checklist

1. Reserve cluster via perf-lab on-call and tag it: perf-mnibp-<gpu>-v1.
2. Ensure node images match release candidate (runtime and driver versions captured in test metadata).
3. Validate telemetry pipeline (traces, kernel histograms, nvlink counters) and TTLs.
4. Import canonical prompt set for fidelity evaluation (see Fidelity Prompts section).
5. Upload test harness artifact to artifacts.redwood/corp/perf/mnibp/<run-id>.

Run procedure (step-by-step)

1. Bootstrap cluster snapshot: run infra snapshot script and pin runtime binaries.
2. Start background telemetry collection: 

   - command: ./tools/telemetry/collect --dest s3://redwood-perf/mnibp/<run-id> --profiles kernel,request,device --sampler deterministic

3. Deploy tenants: primary (target tenants) and noisy tenants using the manifest pattern below.

   - example manifest (YAML):

     tenants:
       - id: target-1
         model: gpt-4x-lite
         concurrency: 8
       - id: noisy-1
         model: noop-stresser
         concurrency: 64

   - apply: ./tools/tenants/deploy --manifest mnibp-manifest.yml --cluster perf-mnibp-<gpu>-v1

4. Run baseline measurement (no noisy tenants) for 10 minutes and store baseline artifacts.
5. Execute noise scenario with parameterized ramp (see Ramp schedule).
6. Capture short-term and long-term metrics (see Metrics and Artifacts).

Ramp schedule examples

- Linear ramp: 0 -> target noisy load over 30s, hold 5 minutes, ramp down 30s.
- Spike ramp: instantaneous jump to 2x noisy load for 15s, then hold at target.
- Random microburst: Poisson arrivals with lambda configured to match observed customer microburst profile.

Metrics and artifacts to collect

- Latency histograms per-tenant (P50/P95/P99) broken down by kernel stage.
- Kernel execution time distributions and stall counts.
- KV-cache hit ratio and eviction timestamps.
- Model fidelity snapshots: per-prompt BLEU/ROUGE/embedding cosine similarity and hallucination count (binary classifier).
- Cost proxies: GPU cycles consumed, kernel occupancy, and per-request energy estimate.
- Traces correlating request -> kernel -> device counters.

Required pass/fail criteria for release gating

- Isolation sanity: under moderate noisy_tenant_load=0.5, target tenants must keep P95 latency <= 1.5x baseline and P99 <= 2.5x baseline.
- Fidelity containment: median fidelity metric must remain within 95% of baseline for text-gen prompts.
- Recovery: after ramp-down, P95 must return to <=1.2x baseline within 120s.
- Observability completeness: telemetry must have >=98% of kernel spans and >=99% of request traces for sampled requests.

Analysis and reporting template

Include these sections in every run report:

- Executive summary (one paragraph): high-level outcome and gate pass/fail.
- Environment snapshot: runtime version, driver, cluster_tag, scheduler_profile.
- Scenario matrix: parameters used and duration.
- Key charts: latency CDFs, kernel latency heatmaps, KV-hit timelines, fidelity drift plots.
- Root-cause hypothesis: annotated with trace IDs and kernel spans.
- Actionable items: owner, priority, ETA.

Example CLI to produce automated report

./tools/perf/report --run-id <run-id> --output reports/mnibp-<run-id>.html --include fidelity,latency,kernel

Fidelity prompts and evaluation guidance

- Use the canonical fidelity set (fidelity-v2) stored in corp/prompts/fidelity-v2.tar.gz.
- Evaluate text-gen with top-n token divergence and an hallucination classifier. Provide both absolute metrics and relative delta to baseline.

Safety and scheduler experiment notes

- Do not enable experimental kernel plugins unless explicitly approved by kernel-safety on-call.
- When testing aggressive preemption policies, ensure a rescue path (canary rollback manifest and immediate disable flag for the scheduler).

Automated ingestion and dashboards

- Test harness must upload JSON artifact with the following top-level fields: run_id, scenario, cluster_tag, timestamps, metrics_uri. (See ingestion schema in corp/perf/ingest-schema.md).
- Dashboards: create a runtime-mnibp-<run-id> dashboard via ./tools/dash/create --template mnibp --source s3://redwood-perf/mnibp/<run-id>

Post-run forensic playbook (if SLOs violated)

1. Triaging: collect top 10 request traces that saw highest kernel stall time.
2. Correlate with kernel load and nvlink errors.
3. Re-run with narrower isolation windows (single noisy tenant) to check for combinatorial effects.

Appendix A: sample JSON artifact (abbreviated)

{
  "run_id": "mnibp-2026-06-01-01",
  "scenario": "burststorm",
  "cluster_tag": "perf-mnibp-a100-v1",
  "metrics_uri": "s3://redwood-perf/mnibp/mnibp-2026-06-01-01/metrics.json",
  "pass": "false"
}

Appendix B: kernel-noise injector (simple example)

// C-style pseudo-code to run on a micro-benchmark tenant
for (i=0; i<100000; i++) {
  heavy_compute_kernel();
  if (i % 37 == 0) sleep_random(0, 300); // introduce jitter in microseconds
}

Appendix C: troubleshooting checklist

- If traces are missing: check telemetry-level and agent config; verify s3 write permissions.
- If kernel histograms look flat: confirm kernel instrumentation was compiled with trace hooks.
- If fidelity metrics show unexpected variance: verify prompt set and model weights pinned to baseline.
